hints: Focus on what stays behind when heated, the sodium ions are only in the anhydrous sodium carbonate, not in the water.
Start by finding the actual mass of sodium in the sample using 25.84% of 35.6 g, then convert that to moles with Ar = 23.0.
Remember each mole of Na2CO3 needs two moles of Na+, use that to find moles of carbonate, then subtract its mass from 35.6 g to leave the water.
walkthrough:
**Find the mass of sodium in the sample**

Sodium is our tracer because water contains no sodium. All the sodium must end up in the anhydrous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$\text{mass of Na}^+ = \frac{25.84}{100} \times 35.6 \text{ g} = 9.2 \text{ g}$$

**Convert sodium to moles of anhydrous carbonate**

Now change grams of sodium into moles, then link it to carbonate. There are 2 moles of $\text{Na}^+$ in every 1 mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$\text{moles Na}^+ = \frac{9.2}{23.0} = 0.40 \text{ mol}$$
$$\text{moles Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = \frac{0.40}{2} = 0.20 \text{ mol}$$

**Find mass of anhydrous salt, then water by difference**

Use $M_r$ of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 106.0$ to get its mass. The rest of the original 35.6 g must have been water of crystallisation.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$\text{mass Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 0.20 \times 106.0 = 21.2 \text{ g}$$
$$\text{mass H}_2\text{O given off} = 35.6 - 21.2 = 14.4 \text{ g}$$

options.A: 7.2 g is 0.40 mol of water. This comes from forgetting the 2:1 ratio and assuming 0.40 mol Na+ means 0.40 mol Na2CO3 and 0.40 mol water. In fact 0.40 mol Na+ gives only 0.20 mol Na2CO3.
options.B: 10.6 g is half the correct anhydrous mass. This comes from halving 21.2 g by mistake, or from confusing moles of Na+ with moles of carbonate when calculating the residue.
options.C: 14.4 g is correct. 9.2 g of Na+ is 0.40 mol, which gives 0.20 mol of Na2CO3 with mass 21.2 g. Subtracting from the hydrated mass, 35.6 - 21.2 = 14.4 g of water is lost.
options.D: 21.2 g is the mass of anhydrous Na2CO3 left behind, not the water lost. It is a classic trap where students calculate the residue correctly but forget the final subtraction step.
